stories.title: Today in Korean history
stories.summary: 1946 -- North Korea founds the ruling Workers' Party, the Soviet-backed regime's first official step toward establishing a communist system in the northern part of the Korean Peninsula. 1961 -- Jo Yong-su, 31, president of the progressive daily Minjok Ilbo, receives a death sentence. He is convicted of spying for North Korea. 1973 -- North Korea unilaterally announces the suspension of dialogue with South Korea, citing moves by then President Park Chung-hee to solidify his grip on power by adopting the "Yushin," or revitalizing, Constitution. A year earlier, the Koreas had issued a joint statement after months of secret negotiations, pledging to work together for the peaceful unification of their divided country and reconciliation. 2003 -- South and North Korea agree to cooperate to ensure the profitability of the troubled Mount Kumgang tour program operated by Hyundai Asan, an affiliate of the Hyundai Group, which provides South Koreans access to the scenic North Korean mountain resort. 2013 -- A T-50 trainer jet crashes in southwestern South Korea, killing both pilots aboard. 2014 -- Kim Young-oh, whose 16-year-old daughter was killed in the Sewol ferry sinking on April 16, ends a 46-day hunger strike due to his worsening condition. He had demanded an independent probe into the cause of the sinking, which left more than 300 people dead. 2015 -- South Korea's Red Cross proposes holding working-level talks with its North Korean counterpart on Sept. 7 to discuss the issue of reunions for families separated by the 1950-53 Korean War.

1961 -- Jo Yong-su, 31, president of the progressive daily Minjok Ilbo, receives a death sentence.
He is convicted of spying for North Korea.

1973 -- North Korea unilaterally announces the suspension of dialogue with South Korea, citing moves by then President Park Chung-hee to solidify his grip on power by adopting the "Yushin," or revitalizing, Constitution.
A year earlier, the Koreas had issued a joint statement after months of secret negotiations, pledging to work together for the peaceful unification of their divided country and reconciliation.

2003 -- South and North Korea agree to cooperate to ensure the profitability of the troubled Mount Kumgang tour program operated by Hyundai Asan, an affiliate of the Hyundai Group, which provides South Koreans access to the scenic North Korean mountain resort.
2013 -- A T-50 trainer jet crashes in southwestern South Korea, killing both pilots aboard.
2014 -- Kim Young-oh, whose 16-year-old daughter was killed in the Sewol ferry sinking on April 16, ends a 46-day hunger strike due to his worsening condition.
He had demanded an independent probe into the cause of the sinking, which left more than 300 people dead.
2015 -- South Korea's Red Cross proposes holding working-level talks with its North Korean counterpart on Sept. 7 to discuss the issue of reunions for families separated by the 1950-53 Korean War.

stories.title: PM calls for overhaul of 'organizational culture' of police amid outrage over missing person cases
stories.summary: Prime Minister Han Seong-sook called for measures Thursday to reform the way police handle missing person cases and to overhaul the agency's "organizational culture" amid public outrage over revelations an officer prematurely closed at least two cases with false reports the victims have been confirmed safe. Two people -- one of them a woman in her 30s and the other a man in his 60s -- were both found dead over the past week, months after they were reported missing on the southern island of Jeju, and the officer in question has been arrested for falsely closing their cases. The revelations raised concerns that missing person cases are not investigated seriously and other cases could have been closed in a similar manner, largely because the vast majority of those reported missing return safely. Since the revelations, police have been looking into the handling of all missing person cases across the nation. Earlier this week, President Lee Jae Myung also called for the establishment of an organization tasked with reforming police as the massive law enforcement agency is set to take over greater roles in the wake of a reform measure stripping prosecutors of the right to conduct investigations on their own. On Thursday, the prime minister said she has called in the acting national police chief and other senior police officials and asked them to come up with measures to overhaul the missing person investigation system and more fundamentally, the organizational culture within the police. "There are serious problems with the procedures, sequences and the ways they deal with things and I believe we have to set these straight," Han told reporters, calling the false closing of the missing person cases "very shocking" and "hard to accept." Han said the envisioned organization for police reform is expected to be established outside the police. "Would it be possible to carry out reforms on their own? Reform measures should sound acceptable to whoever hears them," she said. "I think it would be difficult for the organization to be within the agency."

stories.title: Ghent professors challenged expertise of Jason Arday’s plagiarism accuser
stories.summary: Allegations Nathan Cofnas was unqualified for Ghent role and would cause ‘negative impact’ made to senior leaders months ago Nathan Cofnas, the academic who accused Jason Arday of plagiarism , has been accused of having “very limited expertise” for his academic role by professors also working at Ghent University, who say he has a “far-right agenda”. Cofnas secured a postdoctoral research role “on the future of liberalism” at Belgium’s Ghent University in March. Weeks later, Ghent’s department of philosophy and moral sciences handed a 19-page statement to university officials, setting out why it believed it was “improbable” that Cofnas was the best candidate. Continue reading...
